newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh unions say privatisation creates ghost towns.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh unions say privatisation creates ghost towns.

text.p: A senior Kazakh trade union leader on Wednesday criticised the government's rapid sell-off of strategic industries to foreigners, saying privatisation had created a string of impoverished ghost towns.

"Most of the companies in Kazakhstan's energy and extracting industries have already been sold to foreigners at give-away prices," Leonid Solomin, chairman of the Independent Trade Unions Confederation, told a news conference.
"Instead of a state monopoly, we now have a monopoly of foreign capital," he said.
The government is rapidly privatising the energy-rich country's oil and gas enterprises.
The government, under fire over unpaid salaries and pensions, is looking to foreign cash to replenish the former Soviet republic's stretched state coffers.

Officials put foreign direct investment at $3.5 billion for the Central Asian state of 16.9 million. The figure is the second highest per capita foreign investment among Europe's former communist states.

But amid the flurry of tenders and official optimism, thousands of workers from privatised companies have lost their jobs. Some companies have been closed as "some of the new owners try to suck capital out the plants instead of investing in them", Solomin charged.
He said the closure of troubled enterprises in 56 towns -- once busy industrial centres in Soviet times -- had created ghost towns scattered across the vast, empty steppe land.
Solomin said one example was a joint venture between a Swiss company and a non-ferrous metals plant in the town of Kentau in southern Kazakhstan.

He said the enterprise had been at a standstill for five months, its workers on strike since January, because the Swiss company had not covered debts on salaries to workers and had not invested enough capital.
In letters sent to Kazakh Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin and obtained by Reuters, the Swiss company alleged local bureaucrats and local trade unions were using Kentau for political ends.
But Solomin said Kazakh trade unions backed market reforms.
He said Kazakh unions wanted to take over management of enterprises where foreign investment had failed to turn them around.
"This is the only way to get the economy out of crisis," Solomin said. "We want to implement a scheme of popular capitalism."
